# Riemannian tion of Sample-Based Quantum Krylov Solvers for Elliptic Problems: Energy-Norm Guarantees and Duct-Flow Applications

Doyeol (David) Ahn<sup>∗1,2</sup> and Byeongyong Park<sup>1</sup>

<sup>1</sup>Center for Quantum Information Processing, University of Seoul, 163 Seoulsiripdae-ro, Dongdaemun-gu, Seoul 02504, Republic of Korea

<sup>2</sup>Singularity Quantum Inc., 9506 Villa Isle Drive, Villa Park, California 92861, USA

**Abstract**

Sample-based quantum linear solvers measure quantum Krylov states _e_<sup>-_iAT_</sup>|_b_〉 and reconstruct the solution of _Ax=b_ classically on the observed basis states. We develop this approach for positive- definite systems that arise from elliptic partial differential equations. We formulate the sampling in any fixed basis with an efficient transform and reconstruct the solution by a Galerkin solve on the sampled set. For this reconstruction we derive expected and high-probability energy-norm error bounds, a sample complexity in terms of the smallest sampling probability on an essential set, a computable residual certificate, and a support-completeness theorem for the dephased outcome law. We formulate the method for elliptic problems on Riemannian cross sections. In two dimensions the stiffness matrix is metric-independent in conformal coordinates, and curved vessels lead to the same matrix class. Killing symmetries of the cross section give selection rules for the measurement outcomes, and the Lie derivative of the metric gives first-order bounds for geometric perturbations. As examples we treat the implicit step of pulsatile flow in elliptic, lens-shaped, and curved ducts. In simulations of up to 12 qubits, the number of Fourier modes required for 1% error grows from 14 to 60 while the number of unknowns grows from 64 to 4096. A classical residual-greedy selection is nevertheless more efficient than quantum sampling in all cases studied. On trapped-ion and superconducting processors with six and eight qubits, the outcome laws follow a replacement-noise model whose noiseless fraction decays by about 0.6% per logical two-qubit gate on both platforms, and a parity selection rule rejects shots at the predicted rate. At these sizes the samples cover nearly the whole admissible space, so the experiments test the outcome laws but not dimension reduction.

### 1 Introduction

Many problems in science and engineering lead to large linear systems _Ax=b_. Quantum algorithms for this task began with the algorithm of Harrow, Hassidim, and Lloyd [1] and were improved by later methods based on linear combinations of unitaries and quantum signal processing [2]. These algorithms prepare the solution as a quantum state. In order to read out the solution, however, one must estimate many amplitudes, and the required circuits are deep. Variational methods [3, 4] use shallow circuits, but they rely on a classical optimization without guarantees.

Sample-based methods take a different route. In sample-based quantum diagonalization (SQD), a quantum processor generates bitstrings, and a classical computer diagonalizes the Hamiltonian in the subspace spanned by these bitstrings [5]. Its performance depends on recovery procedures that repair noisy samples by using constraints visible in the measurement outcomes, such as particle-number symmetry [5]. These procedures have been extended to strongly correlated systems [6] and, through code-space<tbc>

<tbc>recovery, to problems without a native constraint \[7\]. Sample-based Krylov quantum diagonalization (SKQD) uses time-evolved states \(e^{-iHT}|\psi\rangle\) as the source of the bitstrings and comes with convergence guarantees \[8\]. The same idea applies to linear systems: one measures quantum Krylov states _e_<sup>-_iAT_</sup>|_b_〉 generated by the Hermitian matrix _A_ itself and solves the system classically on the observed basis states. A related approach was developed concurrently by Park _et al._ \[9\], who apply sample-based Krylov diagonalization to general Hermitian linear systems with a variational reconstruction based on the cost Hamiltonian and prove support-discovery guarantees for that setting. The present paper is self-contained. We treat positive-definite systems from elliptic partial differential equations and reconstruct the solution by a Galerkin solve. The energy-norm bounds of Sec. 3 are derived directly from the outcome law and do not rely on the sampling theorems of Ref. \[9\].

In this paper we develop the method for linear systems that arise from elliptic partial differential equations. These systems are positive definite, and their solutions are smooth. Two observations guide the work. First, the solution of such a system is not concentrated in the grid-point basis, but it is strongly concentrated in a sine or cosine basis matched to the boundary conditions. We therefore measure in such a basis. Second, for a positive-definite system a Galerkin solve on the sampled set is simpler than a variational reconstruction and is optimal in the energy norm. We derive error bounds for this reconstruction and relate them to the sampling probabilities.

Elliptic problems on curved domains are naturally formulated on a Riemannian manifold \[10, 11\]. A cross section with coordinates _u<sup>i</sup>_ carries a metric _g<sub>ij</sub>_, and the physical operator becomes a weighted Laplace-Beltrami operator. In this language a change of coordinates is a diffeomorphism, and the weak form of the problem is invariant under it. The metric then enters the discrete matrix only through the combinations \(\sqrt{g}g^{ij}\) and \(\sqrt{g}\). In two dimensions the first combination is invariant under conformal changes of the metric, which makes the stiffness matrix independent of the geometry. Symmetries of the cross section are isometries generated by Killing fields _X_ with L_<sub>X</sub>g_=0, where L_<sub>X</sub>_ is the Lie derivative. They give selection rules that tell us which measurement outcomes can be discarded. Deformations of the cross section are generated by vector fields _V_ , and the Lie derivative L_<sub>V</sub>g_ gives their first-order effect on the matrix. We use these notions throughout Sec. 4 and summarize them in Appendix A.

We then formulate the method for elliptic problems on a Riemannian cross section. We use the formulation for the implicit step of pulsatile flow in elliptic, lens-shaped, and curved ducts. These ducts are models of compressed and eccentrically narrowed coronary arteries \[12\]. We compare the quantum sampler with classical mode selection, and we test the outcome laws on six- and eight-qubit IonQ and IBM processors. We do not claim a quantum advantage for these examples. The theory and the numerical results instead identify where the sampling is efficient and where it is not.

The contributions of this paper are as follows. (1) We formulate Krylov-state sampling in any fixed basis with an efficient transform (Sec. 2.2). This follows from unitary equivalence, but it is what makes the method useful for partial differential equations. (2) For positive-definite systems we replace the variational reconstruction by a Galerkin solve and derive expected and high-probability energy-norm bounds, a sample complexity, a sampling efficiency, a computable residual certificate, and a support- completeness theorem for the dephased outcome law (Sec. 3). The optimality of the Galerkin solution is the classical Céa property; the new elements are the bounds that connect the energy-norm error to the outcome law. (3) We formulate the method on Riemannian cross sections (Sec. 4). The conformal invariance of the Dirichlet energy, Killing symmetries, and first-order shape calculus are standard tools. Here we use them to identify the matrix class, to construct measurement filters with a guarantee, and to bound the effect of geometric uncertainty. (4) We test the method on elliptic, lens-shaped, and curved ducts in simulation and on two quantum processors (Secs. 5 and 6), and we compare it with classical mode selection at equal subspace size.

The remainder of this paper is organized as follows. Section 2 describes the sampling protocol, measurement in a general basis, and the Galerkin reconstruction. Section 3 derives the energy-norm guarantees, the support-completeness theorem, and the effect of finite time averaging. Section 4 formulates the method on Riemannian cross sections and introduces the duct examples. Section 5 presents numerical results, and Sec. 6 describes the hardware validation on two platforms. ## 2 Sample-based Krylov solver

### 2.1 Problem and sampling protocol

Let \(A=A^\dagger\in\mathbb{C}^{N\times N}\) be invertible, with _N_=2_<sup>n</sup>_ and \(\|b\|=1\). We assume spectral bounds

\(spec(A)\subseteq[-B,-a]\cup[a,B],0<a\le B,\kappa=B/a.\) (1)

The bounds may be conservative. The normalized solution is

\(|x\rangle=\frac{A^{-1}|b\rangle}{\|A^{-1}b\|},\) (2)

and we write \(x_z=\langle z|x\rangle\) for its amplitude at the basis string _z_.

In quantum Krylov-state sampling, each shot prepares \(|b\rangle\), evolves it under _A_ for a time _T_, and measures \(e^{-iAT}|b\rangle\) in the computational basis. If _T_ is drawn from a distribution \(\mu\), the outcome law is

\(q(z)=\mathbb{E}_{T\sim\mu}|\langle z|e^{-iAT}|b\rangle|^2.\) (3)

In this paper \(\mu\) is a finite set of times _T_<sub>1</sub>_,...,T<sub>d</sub>_ with equal or prescribed shot counts. The evolution can be compiled by product formulas or by randomized methods such as qDRIFT \[13\]. Let S be the set of distinct observed strings and S_<sub>M</sub>_ the set observed in _M_ independent shots.

### 2.2 Measurement in a general orthonormal basis

The computational basis is not essential to the protocol. Let _F_ be a unitary matrix with an efficient circuit _F<sub>q</sub>_, and define the basis vectors \(|z\rangle_F=F^\dagger|z\rangle\). Measuring \(F_qe^{-iAT}|b\rangle\) in the computational basis is equivalent to measuring \(e^{-iAT}|b\rangle\) in the basis \(\{|z\rangle_F\}\). Since

\(Fe^{-iAT}F^\dagger=e^{-i\tilde{A}T},\tilde{A}=FAF^\dagger,\tilde{b}=Fb,\) (4)

the protocol in the basis _F_ is the computational-basis protocol for the unitarily equivalent system \(\tilde{A}\tilde{x}=\tilde{b}\). The spectrum, the spectral bounds of Eq. (1), and \(\|A^{-1}b\|\) are unchanged. Therefore every statement about the computational-basis protocol holds in the basis _F_, with _x<sub>z</sub>_ replaced by the coefficients \(\langle z|_Fx\rangle\). We state the results of Sec. 3 directly in the basis _F_. The basis matters because concentration is basis dependent. For elliptic problems with smooth data, a sine or cosine basis matched to the boundary conditions concentrates the solution on a few low wave vectors, whereas the computational (grid-point) basis does not. Sections 4 and 5 use this freedom.

### 2.3 Positive-definite systems and Galerkin reconstruction

When _A_ is Hermitian positive definite, a second reconstruction is available. The duct examples use real symmetric matrices. Let _x_<sup>∗</sup>=_A_<sup>-1</sup>_b_ denote the unnormalized solution, with \(\|b\|=1\), and let \(\hat{x}_z=\langle z|_Fx^*\rangle\) be its coefficients in the measurement basis. For a set S we define \(V_\mathscr{S}=span\{|z\rangle_F:z\in\mathscr{S}\}\). The Galerkin solution \(x_\mathscr{S}\in V_\mathscr{S}\) satisfies \(\langle v,b-Ax_\mathscr{S}\rangle=0\) for all \(v\in V_\mathscr{S}\). With \(\hat{A}=FAF^\dagger\) and \(\hat{b}=Fb\), it is obtained from

\(\hat{A}[\mathscr{S},\mathscr{S}]y=\hat{b}[\mathscr{S}],x_\mathscr{S}=F^\dagger Embed(y,\mathscr{S}),\) (5)

where \(\hat{A}[\mathscr{S},\mathscr{S}]\) is the principal submatrix indexed by S . Since it is a principal submatrix of a positive- definite matrix, Eq. (5) has a unique solution.

**Lemma 1** (Galerkin optimality)**.** _Let_ \(\|v\|_A^2=\langle v,Av\rangle\)_. The Galerkin solution satisfies_ \(\|x_\mathscr{S}-x^*\|_A=min_{v\in V_\mathscr{S}}\|v-x^*\|_A\)_. If_ \(\mathscr{S}\subseteq\mathscr{S}'\)_, then_ \(\|x_{\mathscr{S}^\prime}-x^*\|_A\le\|x_\mathscr{S}-x^*\|_A\).

_Proof._ By substituting _b=Ax_<sup>∗</sup> into the Galerkin condition, we obtain \(\langle v,A(x^*-x_\mathcal{S})\rangle=0\) for all \(v\in V_\mathcal{S}\). Lemma 1 is the classical Céa property \[14\]. For general Hermitian systems one can instead minimize a projected cost function on _V_<sub>S</sub>, as in variational formulations \[4, 15\] and in the solver of Ref. \[9\]. For positive-definite systems the Galerkin solution is simpler: it minimizes the energy-norm error, requires only the principal submatrix \(\hat{A}[\mathcal{S},\mathcal{S}]\), and its error does not increase on nested sets.

### 2.4 A practical solver for positive-definite systems

Algorithm 1 summarizes the variant used in Secs. 4 and 5. Phase 1 measures Krylov states in the basis _F_ with a classical Galerkin solve after each state. Phase 2 is an optional classical expansion that adds the indices with the largest residual components. The function FILTER removes indices at which the solution vanishes by symmetry or constraint, such as a parity rule or a zero mode. A filter must retain every potentially nonzero solution coefficient; discarding physically admissible modes invalidates the coverage bounds. The sampling times may be taken from a uniform grid, whose outcome law approaches the dephased law of Theorem 7 at the rate given by Lemma 9, or from the heuristic schedule of Algorithm 2. The latter is motivated in Sec. 3.2 but carries no separate guarantee.

(9) and the tail condition give the error bound.

Compared with Corollary 3, the high-probability budget replaces \(\mathrm{ln}(2\kappa/\epsilon^2)\) by \(\mathrm{ln}(|\mathscr{E}_\epsilon|/\delta)\). The essential set of Eq. (12) is defined in the energy norm, so it can contain modes of very small normalized weight. Complete discovery of \(\mathscr{E}_\epsilon\) is a sufficient condition and can be pessimistic, because a missed mode of small weight costs little error. Any filter must preserve the solution support, and pruning after sampling must be controlled separately.

**Proposition 5** (Lower bound and sampling efficiency)**.** _Let_ \(K_\epsilon\) _be the smallest_ |S| _for which the Galerkin error is at most_ \(\epsilon\|x^*\|_A\)_. Any sampling protocol needs_ \(M\ge K_\epsilon\) _shots, because each shot adds at most one index. Since_ \(q_\mathrm{min}(\mathscr{E}_\epsilon)\le 1/|\mathscr{E}_\epsilon|\)_, the right-hand side of Eq._ (11) _is at least_ \(|\mathscr{E}_\epsilon|\mathrm{ln}(2\kappa/\epsilon^2)\).

We therefore define the sampling efficiency

\(\eta_\mathrm{s}=|\mathscr{E}_\epsilon|q_\mathrm{min}(\mathscr{E}_\epsilon)\le 1.\) (13)

A small value of \(\eta_\mathrm{s}\) identifies an essential index with a low sampling probability. Inefficiency can arise from repeated samples of already observed indices or from probability mass outside \(\mathscr{E}_\epsilon\). This is a coupon- collector problem with a nonuniform distribution \[16\]. The relevant property of _q_ is its flatness on \(\mathscr{E}_\epsilon\), not its resemblance to \(|\hat{x}|^2\). The two bounds of Proposition 5 need not match when \(\eta_\mathrm{s}\) is small.

**Corollary 6** (Replacement noise)**.** _Suppose that each shot is independently replaced, with probability p\<_1_, by an index drawn from an arbitrary distribution. Then the outcome law satisfies_ \(q'(z)\ge(1-p)q(z)\)_, and the sufficient budget of Corollary 3 increases at most by the factor_ 1/(1-_p)._

By Lemma 1, adding corrupted indices to a retained set cannot increase its error. At a fixed total number of shots, however, replacement can remove useful ideal samples and increase the error relative to an uncontaminated run. The shot bound assumes independent replacement. Arbitrary gate and readout channels need not satisfy the pointwise dominance \(q'\ge(1-p)q\). For them we use a weaker statement. If the actual law \(q'\) lies within total-variation distance \(\eta\) of _q_, then \(|q'(z)-q(z)|\le\eta\) for every _z_, and Corollaries 3 and 4 hold with _q_<sub>min</sub> replaced by \(q_\mathrm{min}-\eta\) whenever this is positive.

For the residual _r=b-Ax_<sub>S</sub>, the identity \(\|x^*-x_\mathscr{S}\|_A^2=r^\dagger A^{-1}r\) gives the computable certificate

\(\frac{\|x^*-x_\mathscr{S}\|_A}{\|x^*\|_A}\le\sqrt{\kappa}\frac{\|r\|}{\|b\|}.\) (14)

Consequently, the residual stopping rule of Algorithm 1 certifies a relative energy error of at most \(\sqrt{\kappa}\varepsilon\), not generally \(\varepsilon\). For an energy tolerance \(\varepsilon_A\) one uses a certified condition-number bound and the residual tolerance \(\varepsilon_A/\sqrt{\kappa}\). Approximate matrix assembly and inexact reduced solves require additional error terms.

## 3.1 Support completeness and dephasing

The following statement explains why a single state can fail and a long time average cannot, and it gives an a priori floor for _q_<sub>min</sub>. We define the dephased law \(q^\infty(z)=\sum_\lambda|a_\lambda(z)|^2\), where the sum runs over the distinct eigenvalues of _A_.

**Theorem 7** (Support completeness)**.** _For every index z,_

\(q^\infty(z)\ge\frac{|\hat{x}_z|^2}{\sum_\lambda\lambda^{-2}}\ge\frac{|\hat{x}_z|^2}{\text{tr}A^{-2}}.\) (15)

_In particular,_ \(\text{supp}\hat{x}\subseteq\text{supp}q^\infty\).

_Proof._ By Eq. (7) and the Cauchy-Schwarz inequality, \(|\hat{x}_z|^2=|\sum_\lambda a_\lambda(z)\lambda^{-1}|^2\le\sum_\lambda|a_\lambda(z)|^2\sum_\lambda\lambda^{-2}\). The sum over distinct eigenvalues is at most the trace of _A_<sup>-2</sup>.

The probability of _z_ in the single state \(|b\rangle\) is \(|\hat{b}_z|^2=|\sum_\lambda a_\lambda(z)|^2\). This sum can vanish by cancellation while \(\hat{x}_z=\sum_\lambda a_\lambda(z)/\lambda\) does not, because the weights \(1/\lambda\) break the cancellation. A classical selection of modes by the magnitude of \(\hat{b}\) has the same deficiency. Section 5.4 shows that this happens for the elliptic duct. For the dephased law, Eq. (15) gives

\(q_\text{min}^\infty(\mathscr{E}_\varepsilon)\ge\frac{\text{min}_{z\in\mathscr{E}_\varepsilon}|\hat{x}_z|^2}{\text{tr}A^{-2}},\) (16)

so that Corollaries 3 and 4 become a priori budgets that depend only on the solution profile and the spectrum. The floor depends on the dimension through tr_A_<sup>-2</sup>, which is dominated by the lowest eigenvalues for elliptic operators. For _A=aI_ the bound is exact.

**Corollary 8** (Constant coefficient)**.** _If every basis vector_ \(|z\rangle_F\) _is an eigenvector of A, then_ \(q(z)=q^\infty(z)=|\hat{b}_z|^2\) _for all sampling times, and_ \(\text{supp}\hat{x}=\text{supp}\hat{b}\).

For uniform times \(T_k=k\Delta t\), _k_=0_,...,d_-1, let \(D_d(\theta)=d^{-1}\sum_{k=0}^{d-1}e^{-ik\theta}\). Expanding the amplitudes in the eigenbasis gives the following lemma, proved in Appendix C.

**Lemma 9** (Finite averaging)**.**

\(|q(z)-q^\infty(z)|\le\sum_{\lambda\neq\mu}|a_\lambda(z)||a_\mu(z)|\left|D_d\big((\lambda-\mu)\Delta t\big)\right|,|D_d(\theta)|\le\text{min}\big\{1,\frac{1}{d|\text{sin}(\theta/2)|}\big\}.\) (17)

Equation (17) shows that dephasing requires \(d|\text{sin}((\lambda-\mu)\Delta t/2)|\gg 1\) for the eigenvalue pairs that carry the solution. The required window depends on the relevant eigenvalue differences and on aliasing, not on \(\lambda_\text{min}\) alone, and near-degenerate pairs may require windows much longer than \(2\pi/\lambda_\text{min}\). The step \(\Delta t=\pi/\lambda_\text{max}\), which we use as the reference short step, gives a total time that is shorter than \(2\pi/\lambda_\text{min}\) by a factor of about \(2\kappa/d\). A single grid can fail completely: if \((\lambda-\mu)\Delta t\) is a multiple of \(2\pi\) for every eigenvalue pair with \(a_\lambda(z)a_\mu(z)\neq 0\), then _D<sub>d</sub>_=1 for these pairs and \(q(z)=|\hat{b}_z|^2\), so a mode hidden by cancellation in \(\hat{b}\) stays hidden. Incommensurate or varied time steps avoid this failure.

### 3.2 Schedule mixtures and a multiscale heuristic

A long uniform step aliases the high eigenvalues, while a short step does not dephase the low ones. An explicit mixture of candidate schedules has the following coverage property.

**Lemma 10** (Schedule mixtures)**.** _Let_ T<sub>1</sub>_,...,T<sub>r</sub> be complete time schedules with outcome laws q_<sup>(1)</sup>_,...,q_<sup>(_r_)</sup>_, and allocate equal total shots to each schedule. The outcome law of the mixture satisfies_

\(q^\mathrm{mix}=\frac{1}{r}\sum_{j=1}^rq^{(j)}\ge\frac{q^{(j)}}{r}\text{\textit{for every j}}.\)

By Corollary 3, the sufficient budget of the mixture is at most _r_ times that of its best constituent for the same essential set. This compares sufficient bounds, not observed stopping times. Times that occur in several constituents are kept with multiplicity. Algorithm 2 instead selects isolated, logarithmically spaced times. It does not contain the candidate fixed-step schedules, and Lemma 10 does not apply to it. We use it as an empirical heuristic. Its lower time scale \(\pi/\lambda_\mathrm{max}\) avoids aliasing of the highest eigenvalues, and its upper scale \(2\pi/\lambda_\mathrm{min}\) resolves the lowest eigenvalues, which dominate \(\hat{x}\) through the weights \(1/\lambda\) of Eq. (7).

## 4 Geometric formulation

In this section we formulate the solver for elliptic problems on a general Riemannian cross section. We first state the geometric method as a sequence of steps. We then show that the guarantees of Sec. 3 apply to the resulting matrices and classify the approximations that a realization requires. An interpretation of the sampling in terms of Green’s functions is given in Appendix B. Elliptic, lens-shaped, and curved ducts appear at the end of the section as concrete examples.

### 4.1 The geometric method

Let \(\Omega\) be a cross section, and let \(\Phi:R\rightarrow\Omega\) be a coordinate map from a simple coordinate domain _R_, such as a rectangle, a strip, or a quarter rectangle. The map induces a metric _g<sub>ij</sub>_ on _R_. The geometric method consists of five steps.

1. _Coordinates_. Choose \(\Phi\) such that the wall of \(\Omega\) is mapped to coordinate lines of _R_. Conformal maps are preferred in two dimensions (Proposition 12), and orthogonal tube coordinates in curved vessels.

2. _Weak form_. Write the physical problem in the invariant weak form (18). The metric enters only through \(\sqrt{g}\) and _g<sup>ij</sup>_.

3. _Reference operator and basis_. Split the discrete matrix as _A=A_<sub>0</sub>+_V_ , where _A_<sub>0</sub> is a reference operator whose eigenbasis _F_ has an efficient quantum circuit. For a rectangle in conformal coordinates with a constant stiffness coefficient, _A_<sub>0</sub> is the flat stiffness matrix and _F_ is a sine or cosine transform. All mode coupling is then contained in _V_ .

4. _Sampling and reconstruction_. Measure Krylov states in the basis _F_ (Sec. 2.2) with a schedule of Sec. 3.1 or 3.2, apply a filter that encodes the symmetries of \(\Omega\), and reconstruct by the Galerkin solve of Eq. (5).

5. _Approximation_. Replace the exact metric, domain, or circuit by approximations of Class I or Class II (Sec. 4.7).

Steps 1-3 define a discrete model, which already includes discretization and any coordinate truncation. Step 5 separates further model and sampler approximations. Physical accuracy requires control of all these contributions.

## 4.2 Elliptic problems on a Riemannian cross section

Let \(\Omega\) have local coordinates (_u_<sup>1</sup>_,u_<sup>2</sup>) and metric _g<sub>ij</sub>_, and let \(\sqrt{g}=\sqrt{\mathrm{det}g_{ij}}\). We consider the weak problem: find _w_ with _w_=0 on the wall such that

\(\int_R\big(\rho g^{ij}\partial_iw\partial_jv+\gamma wv\big)\sqrt{g}du^1du^2=\int_Rfv\sqrt{g}du^1du^2\) (18)

for all admissible _v_. Here \(\rho>0\) and \(\gamma\ge 0\) are coefficient fields. Equation (18) is the weak form of \(-\nabla_g\cdot(\rho\nabla_gw)+\gamma w=f\), where \(\nabla_g\) denotes the Levi-Civita gradient and divergence \[10\]. A conservative discretization on a coordinate grid gives

\(A=K+C,K=\nabla_h^TW\nabla_h,W=\mathrm{blockdiag}\big(\rho\sqrt{g}[g^{ij}]\big),C=\mathrm{diag}(\gamma\sqrt{g}),b=\mathrm{diag}(\sqrt{g})f.\) (19)

where \(\nabla_h\) is the discrete gradient. For an orthogonal coordinate system \[_g<sup>ij</sup>_\] is diagonal and _K_ is a symmetric five-point stencil.

**Proposition 11** (Structure)**.** _The matrix A of Eq._ (19) _is real symmetric positive definite whenever_ \(\rho>0\), \(\gamma\ge 0\)_, and the wall carries a Dirichlet condition. Therefore the results of Sec. 3 apply to every problem of the form_ (18)_, for any metric and any orthogonal measurement basis._

The implicit Euler step of the unsteady Stokes equation, Eq. (25) below, is the case \(\rho=1\), \(\gamma=\Gamma\), and \(f=\Gamma w^n+G^{n+1}\).

## 4.3 Conformal reduction in two dimensions

**Proposition 12** (Conformal reduction)**.** _If the coordinates are conformal,_ \(g_{ij}=h^2\delta_{ij}\)_, then_ \(\sqrt{g}g^{ij}=\delta^{ij}\)_. As a result, K is the flat stiffness matrix with coefficient_ \(\rho\)_, independent of the metric, and the geometry enters only through_ \(C=\mathrm{diag}(\gamma h^2)\) _and b_=diag(_h_<sup>2</sup>)_f._

_Proof._ In two dimensions \(\sqrt{g}=h^2\) and \(g^{ij}=h^{-2}\delta^{ij}\), so their product is \(\delta^{ij}\).

Proposition 12 is the discrete form of the conformal invariance of the Dirichlet energy in two dimensions. When the coordinate domain is a rectangle and \(\rho=1\), a sine or cosine basis diagonalizes _K_ exactly, and all mode coupling comes from the metric factor _h_<sup>2</sup> through _C_. A proper simply connected planar domain admits a conformal map to the disk. Mapping a physical boundary to a rectangle or a strip requires appropriate boundary treatment, and corners, narrow features, and mapping singularities can affect numerical conditioning. Patient-specific cross sections segmented from images can be treated by a numerical conformal map \[17, 18\], which replaces the analytic _h_<sup>2</sup> of the examples below by a computed one.

## 4.4 Symmetries and the Lie derivative

Step 4 of the geometric method applies a filter that removes indices at which the solution vanishes. The Lie derivative gives a systematic way to find such indices. A vector field _X_ on \(\Omega\) is a Killing field if L_<sub>X</sub>g_=0, where L_<sub>X</sub>_ denotes the Lie derivative (Appendix A). Its flow is then a one-parameter group of isometries. A reflection that maps \(\Omega\) onto itself and preserves _g_ is a discrete isometry.

**Proposition 13** (Symmetry selection rule)**.** _(i) Let X be a Killing field that is tangent to the wall and has a complete flow on_ \(\Omega\)_, and assume_ \(\mathcal{L}_X\rho=\mathcal{L}_X\gamma=0\)_. Then_ L_<sub>X</sub> commutes with the solution operator of Eq._ (18)_. In particular, if_ L_<sub>X</sub>f_=0_, then_ L_<sub>X</sub>w_=0_, and if_ -_i_L_<sub>X</sub>f=mf, then_ -_i_L_<sub>X</sub>w=mw._

_(ii) Let P be a unitary matrix with PA=AP and_ \(Pb=\chi b\)_. Then every Krylov state e_<sup>-_iAT_</sup>_b and the solution x_<sup>∗</sup> _are eigenvectors of P with eigenvalue_ \(\chi\)_. If the measurement basis F diagonalizes P, with_ \(FPF^\dagger=\mathrm{diag}(\chi_z)\)_, then q(z_)=0 _and_ \(\hat{x}_z=0\) _for every index with_ \(\chi_z\neq\chi\).

_Proof._ (i) Let \(\phi_s\) be the flow of _X_. Since \(\phi_s\) is an isometry that maps \(\Omega\) and its wall onto themselves and preserves \(\rho\) and \(\gamma\), the bilinear form of Eq. (18) satisfies \(a(\phi_s^*w,\phi_s^*v)=a(w,v)\), and similarly for the load. Hence \(\phi_s^*w\) is the solution for the load \(\phi_s^*f\). By differentiating at _s_=0, we obtain that L_<sub>X</sub>w_ is the solution for the load L_<sub>X</sub>f_. The two statements follow from the linearity and uniqueness of the solution. (ii) Since _P_ commutes with _A_, it commutes with _e_<sup>-_iAT_</sup> and with _A_<sup>-1</sup>. Hence \(Pe^{-iAT}b=\chi e^{-iAT}b\) and \(Px^*=\chi x^*\). For a vector _v_ with \(Pv=\chi v\), we have \(\chi_z(Fv)_z=(FPF^\dagger Fv)_z=\chi(Fv)_z\), so (_Fv)<sub>z</sub>_=0 when \(\chi_z\neq\chi\).

Part (ii) is the discrete form of part (i). It requires a grid that is mapped onto itself by the isometry, so that _P_ is a permutation of grid points. Part (ii) also shows that a filter that keeps the indices with \(\chi_z=\chi\) satisfies the requirement of Algorithm 1: it removes only shots that the ideal sampler never produces and keeps every coefficient that can be nonzero. The parity filter of the lens (Sec. 4.8) is this rule for the two reflections \(\sigma\rightarrow 2\pi-\sigma\) and \(\tau\rightarrow-\tau\). For the disk, the Killing field \(\partial_\vartheta\) restricts a rotationally symmetric load to the modes with zero angular momentum. Conversely, if a coefficient field is not invariant, the selection rule is lost. In a curved vessel the coefficient \(\rho=H\) is not invariant under one of the reflections, and Sec. 5.7 shows that the number of nonzero modes doubles.

## 4.5 Curved and twisted vessels

For a vessel whose centerline has curvature \(\kappa_c\) and torsion \(\tau_c\), we use the orthogonal tube coordinates of Germano \[19\]. In these coordinates the metric is orthogonal, and the effect of torsion on the axial flow appears only at second order \[19\]. Let \(H=1-\kappa_c\rho cos\vartheta\) be the metric factor along the centerline, where \((\rho,\vartheta)\) are polar coordinates in the cross section and _H\>_0 is required throughout the tube. In the Stokes limit, with the secondary flow neglected, we use the reduced scalar model of the form (18) with

\(\rho=H,\gamma=\Gamma H+\frac{\kappa_c^2}{H}.\) (20)

The secondary (Dean) flow \[20\] enters through the convective terms. In an implicit-explicit scheme these terms are moved to the right-hand side, so that the matrix remains of the form (19). Unlike the conformal case, the curvature enters the stiffness matrix through \(\rho=H\). By Proposition 11, the theory applies to this positive-definite reduced model. Its reaction term and load conventions require independent validation against the full vector Stokes equations before quantitative curved-vessel predictions are claimed. Torsion and secondary-flow effects are not validated by the tests of Sec. 5.7.

## 4.6 Spectral bounds from the geometry

The time schedules of Sec. 3.1 and the residual certificate of Eq. (14) require the bounds _a_ and _B_ of Eq. (1). The following proposition supplies them from the geometry alone.

**Proposition 14** (Spectral bounds)**.** _Let C be diagonal with entries in_ \[_c_min_,c_max\]_. Then_

\(\lambda_\mathrm{min}(K)+c_\mathrm{min}\le\lambda_\mathrm{min}(A)\le\lambda_\mathrm{max}(A)\le\lambda_\mathrm{max}(K)+c_\mathrm{max}.\) (21)

_For conformal coordinates on a rectangle of side lengths L_<sub>1</sub>_,L_<sub>2</sub> _with N interior points per direction and_ \(\rho=1\)_, the eigenvalues of K are_ \(\sum_{j=1,2}(4/\Delta_j^2)\mathrm{sin}^2(\pi k_j/(2N+2))\) _with_ \(\Delta_j=L_j/(N+1)\).

_Proof._ For any unit vector _v_, \(\langle v,Av\rangle=\langle v,Kv\rangle+\langle v,Cv\rangle\), and both terms lie between the extreme eigenvalues of the respective matrix.

For the lens of Sec. 4.8 with _N_=32 and \(\Gamma=100\), Eq. (21) gives \(a=2.32\le\lambda_\mathrm{min}=3.07\) and \(\lambda_\mathrm{max}=1045\le B=1062\). For the disk it gives \(1.07\le 1.83\) and \(509\le 552\). These certified values can be used directly in Eq. (1). Weyl’s law \[21\] states that the number of eigenvalues below \(\lambda\) grows as \(|\Omega|_g\lambda/(4\pi)\), where \(|\Omega|_g\) is the area. It is a high-frequency asymptotic statement and does not certify low-lying gaps or a finite dephasing window.

## 4.7 Approximation hierarchy

A realization on hardware requires approximations. We divide them into two classes.

### Class I: approximations of the operator.

These replace _A_ by a nearby matrix \(\tilde{A}\). Examples are the error of a numerical conformal map, the truncation of an infinite coordinate strip, the neglect of higher orders in the curvature, and the penalization of a domain on a bounding box. They change the solution that the algorithm computes.

**Proposition 15** (Metric perturbation)**.** _Let_ \(\tilde{A}=A+\delta A\) _with_ \(|\langle v,\delta Av\rangle|\le\epsilon\langle v,Av\rangle\) _for all v and some_ \(\epsilon<1\)_, and let_ \(\tilde{b}=b+\delta b\) _and_ \(\tilde{x}=\tilde{A}^{-1}\tilde{b}\)_. Then_

\(\frac{\|\tilde{x}-x^*\|_A}{\|x^*\|_A}\le\frac{\epsilon+\|\delta b\|_{A^{-1}}/\|x^*\|_A}{1-\epsilon}.\) (22)

_In particular, a relative error_ \(|\delta\big(\sqrt{g}\big)|\le\epsilon\sqrt{g}\) _of the metric factor in C, or_ \(|\delta\rho|\le\epsilon\rho\) _in K, satisfies the assumption on_ \(\delta A\).

_Proof._ Let \(\mathscr{E}=A^{-1/2}\delta AA^{-1/2}\), so that \(\|\mathscr{E}\|\le\epsilon\). Since \(\tilde{x}-x^*=-\tilde{A}^{-1}\delta Ax^*+\tilde{A}^{-1}\delta b\), we obtain \(A^{1/2}(\tilde{x}-x^*)=-(I+\mathscr{E})^{-1}\mathscr{E}A^{1/2}x^*+(I+\mathscr{E})^{-1}A^{-1/2}\delta b\). Hence \(\|\tilde{x}-x^*\|_A\le(1-\epsilon)^{-1}(\epsilon\|x^*\|_A+\|\delta b\|_{A^{-1}})\). The second statement follows because \(0\unknown C\unknown A\) and \(0\unknown K\unknown A\).

Geometric uncertainty, such as an error in the segmented wall of a vessel, is a Class I approximation of a particular kind. We describe it by a vector field _V_ that deforms the cross section. Its flow \(\psi_s\) maps the reference cross section to the deformed one. By pulling the problem back to the reference coordinates, we keep the grid and the basis _F_ and change only the metric, \(g\rightarrow\psi_s^*g=g+s\mathscr{L}_Vg+O(s^2)\).

**Proposition 16** (First-order shape perturbation)**.** _In two dimensions, let_ \(\mu_1\ge\mu_2\) _be the eigenvalues of g_<sup>-1</sup>L_<sub>V</sub>g at each point. To first order in s, the deformation changes the coefficients of Eq._ (19) _by_

\(\delta\big(\sqrt{g}g^{ij}\big)=-s\sqrt{g}\big(\mathscr{L}_Vg\big)_\circ^{ij},\delta\sqrt{g}=s\sqrt{g}\mathrm{div}_gV,\) (23)

_where_ \((\mathscr{L}_Vg)_\circ=\mathscr{L}_Vg-(\mathrm{div}_gV)g\) _is the trace-free part and indices are raised with g. Hence Proposition 15 applies, to first order, with_

\(\epsilon=|s|\mathrm{max}\big\{\mathrm{sup}_\Omega\frac{1}{2}(\mu_1-\mu_2),\mathrm{sup}_\Omega\frac{1}{2}|\mu_1+\mu_2|\big\},\) (24)

_and with_ \(\delta b=s\mathrm{diag}(\mathrm{div}_gV)b\)_, when_ \(\rho\), \(\gamma\)_, and f are transported with the deformation. A conformal deformation,_ \(\mathscr{L}_Vg=2\sigma g\)_, leaves K unchanged and changes only C and b._

_Proof._ We use \(\delta g^{ij}=-g^{ik}\delta g_{kl}g^{lj}\) and \(\delta\sqrt{g}=\frac{1}{2}\sqrt{g}g^{kl}\delta g_{kl}\) with \(\delta g=s\mathscr{L}_Vg\). Since \((\mathscr{L}_Vg)_{ij}=\nabla_iV_j+\nabla_jV_i\), we have \(\frac{1}{2}g^{kl}(\mathscr{L}_Vg)_{kl}=\mathrm{div}_gV\) . By substituting these expressions into \(\delta(\sqrt{g}g^{ij})=\delta\sqrt{g}g^{ij}+\sqrt{g}\delta g^{ij}\), we obtain Eq. (23). Relative to _g_, the trace-free part has the eigenvalues \(\pm\frac{1}{2}(\mu_1-\mu_2)\), and \(\mathrm{div}_gV=\frac{1}{2}(\mu_1+\mu_2)\). The relative changes of the blocks of _W_ and of the entries of _C_ are therefore bounded by the two terms of Eq. (24), and the bound on \(\langle v,\delta Av\rangle\) follows as in the proof of Proposition 15. For \(\mathscr{L}_Vg=2\sigma g\) the trace-free part vanishes.

The stiffness matrix thus responds only to the shear part of the deformation, and the reaction term and the load respond only to the change of area. This is the infinitesimal form of Proposition 12.

A pointwise relative metric bound does not imply the same relative bound on a signed or cancelling load, so the load term must be estimated separately. A Class I approximation that is itself derived from a weak form of the type (18), with \(\rho>0\) and \(\gamma\ge 0\), preserves positive definiteness and therefore Lemma 1. This is analogous to the conserving approximations of many-body theory, which are derived from a functional and therefore preserve the conservation laws \[22\].

### Class II: approximations of the sampler.

These change only the states that are measured. Examples are qDRIFT compilation \[13\], the Trotter splitting of Eq. (29), truncated Walsh series of diagonal phases, approximate state preparation, gate errors, and readout errors. They do not change _A_ or _b_.

**Corollary 17** (Sampler approximations)**.** _Class II approximations leave the Galerkin solution on a given set unchanged. They affect the outcome law, and Theorem 2 and Corollaries 3 and 4 hold with the law that the approximate sampler actually produces._

Circuit approximations can nevertheless destroy essential support. If an essential mode has zero probability, no finite shot budget recovers it without a separate classical expansion. At a fixed budget, both the achieved accuracy and the classical subspace cost can worsen. The hierarchy gives a simple design rule. The accuracy budget is spent on Class I, where Proposition 15 applies. Class II approximations cost shots and coverage, and their effect enters only through the outcome law.

## 4.8 Examples: elliptic, lens-shaped, and curved ducts

We now apply the geometric method to three cases. The first two are exact conformal instances. The third uses the curvature terms of Sec. 4.5 and is treated numerically in Sec. 5.7.

### 4.8.1 The implicit step in conformal coordinates

We consider fully developed axial flow _w(x,y,t_) in a straight duct driven by a pressure gradient _G(t_). Let (_u,v_) be conformal coordinates of the cross section with scale factor _h(u,v_), so that \(\nabla^2=h^{-2}(\partial_{uu}+\partial_{vv})\). We nondimensionalize lengths by a geometric length \(\ell_g\), the velocity by \(G\ell_g^2/\mu\), and time by \(\ell_g^2/v\). The implicit Euler step of the unsteady Stokes equation then reads

\(-(\partial_{uu}+\partial_{vv})w^{n+1}+\Gamma h^2w^{n+1}=h^2\big(\Gamma w^n+G^{n+1}\big),\Gamma=\frac{\ell_g^2}{v\Delta t}.\) (25)

The operator is symmetric positive definite, and its variable coefficient _h_<sup>2</sup> is supplied by the geometry. For \(\Gamma=0\), Eq. (25) reduces to steady Poiseuille flow with a constant-coefficient operator, to which Corollary 8 applies. For a coronary artery with \(\ell_g\approx 1.3-1.5\) mm, \(v=3.3\times 10^{-6}\) m<sup>2</sup>/s, and one hundred steps per cardiac cycle (\(\Delta t=8\) ms), we obtain \(\Gamma\approx 64-85\). We therefore study \(\Gamma=0\), 100, and 1000.

### 4.8.2 Elliptic duct

Elliptic coordinates are \(x=\ell_g\mathrm{cosh}\mu\mathrm{cos}v\), \(y=\ell_g\mathrm{sinh}\mu\mathrm{sin}v\), with \(h^2=\ell_g^2(\mathrm{sinh}^2\mu+\mathrm{sin}^2v)\), where \(\ell_g\) is half the distance between the foci. The wall is \(\mu=\mu_0\), with semi-axes \(A_e=\ell_g\mathrm{cosh}\mu_0\) and \(B_e=\ell_g\mathrm{sinh}\mu_0\). We use _B<sub>e</sub>/A<sub>e</sub>_=0.5. In order to avoid the branch line at the focal segment, we solve on the quarter domain \(0\le\mu\le\mu_0\), \(0\le v\le\pi/2\). The focal segment and the two axes are symmetry lines with zero normal derivative, and the wall carries _w_=0. On a cell-centered grid with _N_=2_<sup>m</sup>_ points per direction, the one-dimensional Laplacians are diagonalized exactly by the DCT-IV in \(\mu\) and the DCT-II in _v_. The measurement basis is \(F=\mathrm{DCT}-\mathrm{IV}\otimes\mathrm{DCT}-\mathrm{II}\) on 2_m_ qubits. The steady solution is known in closed form \[23\],<tbc>

\(w=\frac{A_e^2B_e^2}{2(A_e^2+B_e^2)}\big(1-\frac{x^2}{A_e^2}-\frac{y^2}{B_e^2}\big),Q=\frac{\pi A_e^3B_e^3}{4(A_e^2+B_e^2)}.\) (26)

<tbc>Since _h_<sup>2</sup> is a sum of a function of \(\mu\) and a function of _v_, the operator of Eq. (25) is separable,

\(A=A_\mu\otimes I+I\otimes A_v,A_\mu=-\partial_{\mu\mu}+\Gamma\mathrm{sinh}^2\mu,A_v=-\partial_{vv}+\Gamma\mathrm{sin}^2v.\) (27)

The continuous counterparts of \(A_\mu\) and _A<sub>v</sub>_ are the modified and ordinary Mathieu operators \[24\]. Separability has three consequences. First, the system is solved classically by two \(N\times N\) eigenvalue problems. Second, \(e^{-iAT}=e^{-iA_\mu T}\otimes e^{-iA_vT}\), so no entangling gate between the registers is needed for the time evolution. Third, the source _h_<sup>2</sup> has Schmidt rank 2, and the product evolution preserves this rank. Each<tbc>

Krylov circuit therefore consists of one _R<sub>Y</sub>_ rotation that prepares \(s_1|0\rangle+s_2|1\rangle\) on the first qubit, one CNOT gate to the second register, and two _m_-qubit unitaries

\(W_\mu=\mathrm{DCT}_4e^{-iA_\mu T}U_u,W_\nu=\mathrm{DCT}_2e^{-iA_\nu T}U_v,\) (28)

where _U<sub>u</sub>_ and _U<sub>v</sub>_ map \(|0\rangle,|1\rangle\) to the Schmidt vectors of the source. The circuit is exact, and its depth does not depend on _T_. This makes the elliptic duct a structured calibration benchmark. On the other hand, generic synthesis of \(W_\mu\) and _W<sub>v</sub>_ has a cost exponential in the register size, so separability alone does not supply an efficient asymptotic quantum algorithm, and the problem is classically easy.

### 4.8.3 Lens-shaped duct

Bipolar coordinates are \(x=\ell_g\mathrm{sinh}\tau/(\mathrm{cosh}\tau-\mathrm{cos}\sigma),y=\ell_g\mathrm{sin}\sigma/(\mathrm{cosh}\tau-\mathrm{cos}\sigma)\), with \(h=\ell_g/(\mathrm{cosh}\tau-\mathrm{cos}\sigma)\). A curve of constant \(\sigma\) is a circular arc through the foci \((\pm\ell_g,0)\). The lens is the region \(\sigma_0\le\sigma\le 2\pi-\sigma_0\), whose corners at the foci have the interior angle \(W_c=2\pi-2\sigma_0\). For \(\sigma_0=\pi/2\) the lens is a disk of radius \(\ell_g\). We use \(\sigma_0=2\pi/3\), which gives corners of \(120^\circ\). The strip \(-\infty<\tau<\infty\) is truncated to \(|\tau|\le\tau_\mathrm{max}\) with _w_=0 at \(\tau=\pm\tau_\mathrm{max}\). It can be shown that the homogeneous solutions decay as \(e^{-\pi|\tau|/W_c}\) toward the corners, so the truncation error is exponentially small. We use \(\tau_\mathrm{max}=6\). With Dirichlet conditions on all sides and _N_ interior points, the basis is \(F=\mathrm{DST}-\mathrm{I}\otimes\mathrm{DST}-\mathrm{I}\).

The lens and the source are symmetric about \(\sigma=\pi\) and \(\tau=0\). Therefore only modes with odd indices in both directions are excited. This symmetry sector has dimension _N_<sup>2</sup>/4. Symmetry alone does not make every coefficient in the sector nonzero. This is the selection rule of Proposition 13 for the two reflections of the lens. In the quantum register this sector corresponds to the least significant qubit of each register being 0, and a measured bitstring that violates this rule can be discarded. This parity filter plays the role of particle-number postselection in SQD \[5\].

The lens operator is not separable. We use the split Trotter step

\(e^{-i\Lambda\Delta t/r}\approx F_q^\dagger D_\Lambda F_qD_h,D_\Lambda=e^{-i\Lambda_0\Delta t/r},D_h=e^{-i\Gamma\mathrm{diag}(h^2)\Delta t/r},\) (29)

where \(\Lambda_0\) contains the eigenvalues of the constant-coefficient Laplacian. Both factors are diagonal in some basis, so no Pauli decomposition of _A_ is needed, and \(D_\Lambda\) is separable between the registers. The splitting is a Class II approximation. On hardware the grid and the transform must be chosen together. With _N_=2_<sup>m</sup>_ interior points the DST-I has the denominator _N_+1, so a power-of-two QFT does not implement it exactly without padding. A cell-centered Dirichlet grid leads to a DST-II with a power-of- two denominator, but it changes the discrete operator and the source. We leave it as a future option. For small registers the DST-I can be synthesized exactly as a generic register unitary, and we use this in the hardware pilot. All numerical results below use the DST-I grid.

### 4.8.4 General and curved cross sections

For a patient-specific cross section, Step 1 is a numerical conformal map onto a rectangle or a disk \[17, 18\]. The analytic _h_<sup>2</sup> of the examples above is then replaced by a computed metric factor, and the map error is a Class I approximation bounded by Proposition 15. If no map is available, a Brinkman penalization on a bounding box \[25\] gives an operator of the same form with a discontinuous coefficient. For a curved vessel, Step 2 uses the coefficients (20). The curvature breaks the symmetry \(\tau\rightarrow-\tau\) of the lens, so that the parity filter acts only in \(\sigma\).

### 5.1 Setup

All results in this section use exact time evolution of the discrete operator and multinomial sampling from the exact outcome laws, without hardware noise unless stated otherwise. We use _d_=12 Krylov states<tbc>

### Support completeness.

4 tests Eq. (15) without a support threshold in the bound itself. The ratio \(q^\infty(z)\text{tr}A^{-2}/|\hat{x}_z|^2\) must be at least 1 for every mode, and it is. We compute \(q^\infty\) with degenerate eigenvalues grouped into spectral projectors (tolerance \(10^{-6}\lambda_\text{max}\)). Without this grouping, exactly degenerate pairs from different symmetry sectors are split and produce spurious weight outside the sector. The same ratio formed with the single-state law \(|\hat{b}_z|^2\) vanishes for the ellipse. For the lens, both \(\hat{b}\) and \(\hat{x}\) lie in the odd-odd sector of dimension _N_<sup>2</sup>/4. The solution coefficients decay rapidly, so the number of modes counted as nonzero depends on the threshold;  4 gives two thresholds. ### Efficiency and initial state.

With the multiscale heuristic, the efficiency of Eq. (13) lies between \(2\times 10^{-3}\) and \(6\times 10^{-2}\). The sampler is therefore 16 to 480 times less efficient than a uniform law on \(\mathscr{E}_\varepsilon\). ## 5.6 Comparison with classical mode selection

Because _b_ and _A_ are known classically, the sampler must be compared with classical selections of the same Galerkin subspace. We consider three. The first selects the modes with the largest \(|\hat{b}_z|\). The second selects the largest \(|\hat{b}_z/\Lambda_{0,z}|\). The third is the residual-greedy method, which starts from the ten largest \(|\hat{b}_z|\) and repeatedly adds the modes with the largest residual, i.e., Phase 2 of Algorithm 1 used alone. Its cost includes residual formation and repeated solves; the efficiency \(\eta_\mathrm{s}\) is not a performance measure for this deterministic method.

8 shows the result for the ellipse at matched |S|. With a suitable uniform step, the Krylov sampling outperforms the first two selections by one to four orders of magnitude. This is the effect of Theorem 7. The residual-greedy method, however, is better than the Krylov sampling in every case, often by several orders of magnitude. For the lens it is at least as good. For an off-center localized source in the lens, the selection by \(|\hat{b}|\) was also better than the Krylov sampling, by a factor of 1.3 to 2.4 in error. These results are consistent with the efficiency analysis and with the remark in Sec. 7 that favorable concentration alone is not evidence of quantum advantage.

## 6 Hardware validation on two platforms

We tested the method on two processors of different technology: the IonQ Forte-1 trapped-ion processor and the IBM superconducting processor `ibm\_cleveland`. We used the \(8\times 8\) grids (six data qubits) of the ellipse and the lens with \(\Gamma=100\) on both processors, and the \(16\times 16\) grids (eight data qubits) on the IBM processor. The six-qubit logical circuits are identical on the two platforms. At these sizes every quantity of Sec. 5 can be computed exactly. The measured outcome laws can therefore be compared with the ideal laws mode by mode. The experiment does not test asymptotic scaling, and it is not intended to show an advantage. With 1500 shots per case, which exceeds the dimension, the sampled sets cover 89 to 100% of the admissible basis. The experiments therefore test the outcome laws, the noise model, and the selection rule. They do not test the reduction of the subspace dimension, which is the purpose of sample-based methods.

### 6.1 Circuits and execution

We used three Krylov states for each duct, with \(T_k=k\Delta t\), _k_=0,1,2, and the geometric-mean step \(\Delta t=\pi/\sqrt{\lambda_{min}\lambda_{max}}\). For the ellipse the operator separates as \(A=A_\mu\otimes I+I\otimes A_\nu\), and the source _h_<sup>2</sup> has Schmidt rank two. Each circuit then consists of a short preparation of the two Schmidt coefficients and one unitary per register. The register unitary combines the Schmidt vectors of _b_, the evolution, and the transform to the cosine basis. The circuits are exact. They contain 38 or 39 logical two-qubit gates for six qubits, below the bound of 41 from generic three-qubit synthesis \[26\], and 191 for eight qubits. These register unitaries are computed from the classical diagonalization of one-dimensional operators. The ellipse circuits therefore test sampling, measurement, and reconstruction under real noise, not a scalable implementation of the time evolution.

For the lens we prepared the source exactly and used one symmetric Trotter step of the split evolution of Sec. 4.8 per circuit. A step consists of register unitaries built from the DST-I and \(e^{-i\Lambda\delta/2}\), and the diagonal phase \(e^{-i\Gamma h^2\delta}\) on all qubits. Thus the noise is not entirely uniform, and the deviation is largest for the strongly concentrated law of the ellipse at _k_=0. For IonQ, a model with independent bit flips on each qubit in addition to uniform replacement reduces the residual to 1.1 to 1.5 times its sampling value, but the fitted flip probabilities vary from circuit to circuit and are not determined reliably by 500 shots. The eight-qubit lens circuits, with 711 to 2975 native two-qubit gates, are fully randomized (_p\>_0.99).

### Parity filter.

For the lens, the measured fraction of shots in the odd-odd sector agrees with the prediction 1-3_p/_4 of the fitted uniform model to within 0.04 for all six-qubit circuits on both platforms. For the fully randomized eight-qubit circuits it approaches the uniform value 1/4, as expected. On IonQ the filter removes about half of all shots and reduces the distance to the circuit law from 0.33 to 0.17 for _k_=0 and from 0.54 to 0.16 for _k_=1. The parity filter therefore acts as a direct and inexpensive noise diagnostic, as anticipated in Sec. 4.4. This use of a measurement-visible constraint is the same mechanism as the particle-number recovery of SQD \[5\] and the code-space recovery of Ref. \[7\]. In the present case the constraint is not engineered; it follows from the isometries of the cross section.

### Dominance.

Corollary 6 predicts \(q_\mathrm{hw}(z)\ge(1-p)q(z)\) for replacement noise. For the pooled six- qubit lens shots, \(\mathrm{min}_{z\in\mathcal{E}_\mathrm{E}}q_\mathrm{hw}(z)/q(z)\) is 0.36 on IonQ and 0.09 on IBM, compared with \(1-\bar{p}=0.35\) and 0.10. For the ellipse the ratio falls below \(1-\bar{p}\) on both platforms: 0.65 versus 0.70 on IonQ, 0.42 versus 0.69 on IBM with six qubits, and 0.14 versus 0.25 on IBM with eight qubits. These violations are consistent with the nonuniform part of the noise, for which the pointwise dominance is not guaranteed. The coverage bounds of Sec. 3 should therefore be applied to hardware data with the measured, not the modeled, outcome law.

## Subspace size and reconstruction.

11 shows that the full hardware samples contain 89 to 100% of the admissible modes. The small Galerkin errors therefore reflect a solve in nearly the whole admissible space, not a reduction of the subspace. Classical residual-greedy selection of the same size is as accurate or more accurate in every case, by up to eight orders of magnitude for the eight-qubit ellipse. Figure 4 compares the reconstructions at equal subspace size over the whole range of budgets. Except where both selections reach the whole sector, the hardware samples are less accurate than residual-greedy selection of the same size by factors from about 2 at the smallest budgets to about 10<sup>8</sup> for the eight-qubit ellipse. The ideal Krylov sampler, by contrast, stays within about one order of magnitude of the greedy and oracle selections for the six-qubit ellipse, although it reaches only small subspaces with these budgets. The loss of efficiency per basis state therefore comes from the hardware noise, which adds modes with negligible solution weight.

The same noise improves coverage per shot at these sizes, because it spreads shots over modes that the ideal law rarely visits. Sample-based methods aim to reduce the subspace, however, so the relevant measure is the error per basis state, and by that measure noise is harmful. A test of dimension reduction requires admissible spaces much larger than the number of distinct samples.

## 7 Discussion

In this method the quantum processor only proposes coordinates. The classical computer then determines their coefficients by a Galerkin solve. The bounds of Sec. 3 relate the outcome law to the exposure of solution coordinates and turn the exposed coordinates into an energy-norm error. For positive-definite systems the Galerkin solve needs only a principal submatrix of \(\hat{A}\), and its error decreases monotonically as the sampled set grows.

The geometric formulation of Sec. 4 shows how these principles apply to linear systems from partial differential equations. The measurement basis matters more than the circuit. For the ducts, a Fourier basis matched to the boundary conditions reduces the subspace by one to two orders of magnitude, and the required number of modes grows slowly with the grid. The time schedule must be chosen for the linear system. The short step that is natural for eigenvalue SKQD fails on fine grids, because it does not dephase the low eigenvalues, whereas the multiscale heuristic improves on the fixed steps in several of our tests. Operator approximations are controlled by Proposition 15, while sampler approximations change coverage, achieved error, and postprocessing cost but not the target.

The examples also make the limitation concrete. In all problems studied, including curved vessels and chaotic cross sections, a classical residual-greedy selection finds the essential modes more efficiently than the quantum sampler. The measured efficiency \(\eta_\mathrm{s}\) lies between \(6\times 10^{-5}\) and \(6\times 10^{-2}\), so rare modes are covered poorly. The elliptic duct and the curved vessels nevertheless exhibit the mechanism by which sampling can help: when the source and the solution have different mode structures, the dephased law captures the solution while a source-based selection does not. A benefit requires that this mismatch occur together with an essential set that no classical method identifies cheaply. -space recovery [7] could supply a recovery signal where native filters are absent, such as the ellipse and the curved vessels. Initial states that flatten the outcome law on the essential set are a direct target for improving \(\eta_\mathrm{s}\).

The hardware experiments add two practical observations. First, the noise on both platforms behaved approximately as the replacement noise of Corollary 6, with a strength set mainly by the number of two-qubit gates. Second, a symmetry selection rule is an inexpensive noise diagnostic: the fraction of rejected lens shots measured the noise strength directly. Such rules exist whenever the cross section has an isometry that preserves the coefficients, and they should be built into the measurement basis where possible. On the other hand, the present experiments do not test the reduction of the subspace, because the number of shots exceeds the admissible dimension. Such a test requires larger registers and shallower circuits.

Several questions remain open. The high-probability bound of Corollary 4 requires complete discovery of an energy-norm essential set, which can be pessimistic; a bound in terms of retained energy would be sharper. The heuristic multiscale schedule performs well in our tests but has no guarantee. Finally, a useful-scale comparison must include classical input access, state preparation, and the full reconstruction cost, with matched accuracy.

## 8 Conclusion

We have developed sample-based quantum Krylov solvers for positive-definite systems from elliptic partial differential equations. We formulated the sampling in any fixed basis with an efficient transform. For the Galerkin reconstruction we derived expected and high-probability energy-norm bounds, a sample<tbc>

complexity, a residual certificate, a support-completeness theorem, and a sampling efficiency. We formulated the method on Riemannian cross sections, showed that conformal coordinates make the stiffness matrix metric-independent in two dimensions, obtained measurement filters from the isometries of the cross section, and bounded the effect of geometric perturbations through the Lie derivative of the metric. Numerical results for elliptic, lens-shaped, and curved ducts confirm the guarantees and show strong compression in a Fourier basis. Experiments on trapped-ion and superconducting processors confirm the measurement convention, the parity selection rule, and the replacement-noise picture.

The analysis and the examples also identify the conditions under which quantum Krylov-state sampling can be expected to offer a benefit. (1) The source and the solution must have different mode structures, so that a selection from the source fails. (2) The essential set must not be identifiable by an inexpensive classical procedure such as residual-greedy selection. (3) The outcome law must be nearly flat on the essential set, so that the sampling efficiency is not small. (4) The hardware noise must be small enough that the samples do not fill the admissible space with modes of negligible solution weight. The elliptic duct and the curved vessels satisfy condition (1). Condition (2) fails in all examples studied here, and condition (4) fails in the present hardware experiments. Problems that satisfy all four conditions remain to be identified.

## A Elements of Riemannian geometry

This appendix summarizes the notions of Riemannian geometry used in Sec. 4. Standard references are Refs. \[10, 11, 21\]. We use the summation convention.

### Metric and volume.

A Riemannian manifold \((\Omega,g)\) is a smooth manifold with a positive-definite symmetric tensor _g<sub>ij</sub>_ in local coordinates _u<sup>i</sup>_. The line element is _ds_<sup>2</sup>=_g<sub>ij</sub>du<sup>i</sup>du<sup>j</sup>_, and _g<sup>ij</sup>_ denotes the inverse matrix. The volume element is \(d\mu_g=\sqrt{g}du^1\cdots du^n\) with \(\sqrt{g}=\sqrt{\mathrm{det}g_{ij}}\). For a map \(\Phi:R\rightarrow\Omega\subset\mathbb{R}^n\) from a coordinate domain, the induced metric is \(g_{ij}=\partial_i\Phi\cdot\partial_j\Phi\).

### Gradient, divergence, and the Laplace-Beltrami operator.

The gradient of a function is \((\nabla_gw)^i=g^{ij}\partial_jw\), and the divergence of a vector field is \(\mathrm{div}_gV=g^{-1/2}\partial_i(\sqrt{g}V^i)\). The weighted operator of Eq. (18) is

\(-\nabla_g\cdot(\rho\nabla_gw)=-\frac{1}{\sqrt{g}}\partial_i\big(\rho\sqrt{g}g^{ij}\partial_jw\big).\) (30)

For \(\rho=1\) it is the Laplace-Beltrami operator \(-\Delta_g\). By multiplying Eq. (30) by a test function _v_ that vanishes on the wall and integrating with \(d\mu_g\), we obtain the left side of Eq. (18). The integrand \(\rho g^{ij}\partial_iw\partial_jv\sqrt{g}\) is a density, so the weak form does not depend on the choice of coordinates.

### Conformal metrics in two dimensions.

If \(g_{ij}=h^2\delta_{ij}\), then \(\sqrt{g}=h^2\) and \(\sqrt{g}g^{ij}=\delta^{ij}\), so that \(\Delta_g=h^{-2}\Delta\) and the Dirichlet energy \(\int g^{ij}\partial_iw\partial_jwd\mu_g\) equals its flat value. This is the content of Proposition 12. The Gaussian curvature of a conformal metric is \(\mathcal{K}=-h^{-2}\Delta\mathrm{ln}h\). A metric induced by a conformal map of a planar domain is flat, so ln_h_ is harmonic. For the elliptic coordinates, \(h^2=\ell_g^2|\mathrm{sinh}(\mu+i\nu)|^2\), and for the bipolar coordinates, \(h=\ell_g/|\mathrm{cosh}\tau-\mathrm{cos}\sigma|\); in both cases ln_h_ is the real part of the logarithm of an analytic function. This identity provides a simple check of a numerically computed metric factor.

### Lie derivative.

Let _X_ be a vector field with flow \(\phi_s\). The Lie derivative of a tensor field _T_ is<tbc>

\(\left.\mathcal{L}_XT=\frac{d}{ds}\right|_{s=0}\phi_s^*T.\) (31)

<tbc>For a function, \(\mathcal{L}_Xw=X^i\partial_iw\). For a vector field, L_<sub>X</sub>Y_=\[_X,Y_\]. For the metric,

\((\mathcal{L}_Xg)_{ij}=X^k\partial_kg_{ij}+g_{kj}\partial_iX^k+g_{ik}\partial_jX^k=\nabla_iX_j+\nabla_jX_i,\) (32)

where \(\nabla\) is the Levi-Civita connection. The trace is _g<sup>ij</sup>_(L_<sub>X</sub>g_)<sub>_ij_</sub>=2div_<sub>g</sub>X_. Pull-back commutes with _d/ds_, so \(\frac{d}{ds}\phi_s^*T=\phi_s^*\mathcal{L}_XT\) for all _s_.

### Killing and conformal Killing fields.

A Killing field satisfies L_<sub>X</sub>g_=0. Its flow consists of isometries, and it commutes with \(\Delta_g\). Examples are \(\partial_\theta\) for a disk in polar coordinates and translations along a straight duct. A conformal Killing field satisfies \(\mathcal{L}_Xg=2\sigma g\) for a function \(\sigma\). In two dimensions every analytic function \(\zeta(u^1+iu^2)\) defines a conformal Killing field of the flat metric, which is why conformal maps are so plentiful in the plane. Proposition 13 uses Killing fields and discrete isometries, and Proposition 16 uses the trace-free part of L_<sub>V</sub>g_, which vanishes exactly for conformal Killing fields.

### Variations of the metric.

For a variation \(\delta g_{ij}\),

\(\delta g^{ij}=-g^{ik}\delta g_{kl}g^{ij},\delta\sqrt{g}=\frac{1}{2}\sqrt{g}g^{kl}\delta g_{kl}.\) (33)

With \(\delta g=s\mathcal{L}_Vg\) these formulas give Eq. (23). A moving wall, as in a pulsating vessel, can be treated in the same way: if the wall moves with velocity _V_ , the pulled-back metric evolves as \(\partial_tg=\mathcal{L}_Vg\), which is the geometric content of an arbitrary Lagrangian-Eulerian formulation.

#### Tube coordinates.

Let a centerline have arc length _s_, curvature \(\kappa_c\), and torsion \(\tau_c\). Let \((\rho,\vartheta)\) be polar coordinates in the normal plane, with \(\vartheta\) measured from a direction that rotates relative to the principal normal by the accumulated torsion angle \(\vartheta_0(s)\), \(|\vartheta'_0|=|\tau_c|\). Germano showed that this choice removes the off-diagonal terms and gives the orthogonal metric \(ds^2=d\rho^2+\rho^2d\vartheta^2+H^2ds^2\), where \(H=1-\kappa_c\rho cos(\vartheta-\vartheta_0)\) \[19\]. Over a short segment, or for \(\tau_c=0\), \(\vartheta_0\) can be set to zero, which gives the factor _H_ of Sec. 4.5. The cross-sectional coefficients of Eq. (20) follow from this metric.

#### Spectral asymptotics.

For the Dirichlet Laplace-Beltrami operator on a two-dimensional domain, Weyl’s law states that the number of eigenvalues below \(\lambda\) grows as \(|\Omega|_g\lambda/(4\pi)\) \[21\]. Since \(|\Omega|_g=\int\sqrt{g}\) is unchanged by a change of coordinates, the high-frequency part of the spectrum does not depend on the coordinate map.

### B.1 Green’s-function interpretation

The sampling laws have a natural interpretation in terms of Green’s functions \[27\]. We regard _A_ as a single-particle Hamiltonian and define, for the basis vector \(|z\rangle_F\) and the source _b_,

\(G_{zb}^\mathrm{prop}(T)=-i\langle z|_Fe^{-iAT}|b\rangle,G_{zb}^R(\omega)=\langle z|_F(\omega-A+i0^+)^{-1}|b\rangle,\rho_{zb}(\omega)=2\pi\sum_\lambda a_\lambda(z)\delta(\omega-\lambda).\) (34)

Here \(\rho_{zb}\) is a cross spectral measure and _G_<sup>prop</sup> is a propagator matrix element. It is not a many-body greater Green’s function, which would require a specified state, field operators, and occupation factors. The resolvent interpretation is exact for the finite matrix without those statistical assumptions.

**Proposition 18** (Green’s-function form)**.** _The quantities of Sec. 3 are_

\(q(z)=\frac{1}{d}\sum_k\big|G_{zb}^\mathrm{prop}(T_k)\big|^2,q^\infty(z)=\mathrm{lim}_{\mathscr{T}\rightarrow\infty}\frac{1}{\mathscr{T}}\int_0^\mathscr{T}\big|G_{zb}^\mathrm{prop}(T)\big|^2dT,\hat{b}_z=\int\frac{d\omega}{2\pi}\rho_{zb}(\omega),\hat{x}_z=-G_{zb}^R(0)=\int\frac{d\omega}{2\pi}\frac{\rho_{zb}(\omega)}{\omega}.\text{(35)}\)

_Proof._ The first relation is Eq. (6). The second follows from \(G_{zb}^\mathrm{prop}(T)=-i\sum_\lambda a_\lambda(z)e^{-i\lambda T}\), since the cross terms with \(\lambda\neq\mu\) average to zero. Equation (36) follows from Eq. (7).

Proposition 18 gives the sampling theory a spectral meaning. The source is the zeroth moment of the cross spectral measure, equal to \(\langle z|_Fb\rangle\), rather than a unit-normalized diagonal spectral sum rule; cross spectral weights can have either sign or be complex. The solution is the static response, that is, the moment of order -1. A single state measures only the zeroth moment, which can vanish by cancellation. The dephased law \(q^\infty\) is the sum of squared cross amplitudes at distinct eigenvalues. It does not measure the signed spectral measure itself. A time window of length T resolves frequencies only to about \(2\pi/\mathscr{T}\) , and the moment of order -1 is dominated by the lowest poles. This motivates the upper time scale of Algorithm 2; actual dephasing requires resolution of the relevant eigenvalue differences, as in Lemma 9. On the other hand, the quantum device returns only intensities \(|G_{zb}^\mathrm{prop}|^2\). The method therefore locates the spectral weight but does not reconstruct the Green’s function, in contrast with the approach of Ref. \[28\].

## B.2 Spectral geometry and sampling efficiency

The efficiency \(\eta_\mathrm{s}\) of Eq. (13) depends on how the eigenvectors of _A_ are spread over the measurement basis, since \(q^\infty(z)=\sum_\lambda|a_\lambda(z)|^2\). In spectral geometry, eigenfunctions of domains with integrable geodesic flow, such as the disk and the ellipse, are structured, while those of chaotic domains, such as the stadium, become equidistributed at high energy \[29-32\]. This suggests a hypothesis: a chaotic cross section might give a flatter _q_, a larger \(\eta_\mathrm{s}\), and an essential set that is harder to find classically. We tested this hypothesis in Sec. 5.7 and found no support for it. A theoretical reason is that quantum ergodicity is a statement about high-lying eigenfunctions, while the solution of an elliptic problem with smooth data is carried by the lowest modes.

### Numerical test.

We tested the hypothesis of Sec. B.2 in two ways. First, we used smooth non-separable conformal deformations of a square, \(h^2=\mathrm{exp}(2\Re\phi)\) with \(\phi\) a random cubic polynomial of amplitude between 0.3 and 1.5. Compared with a separable metric factor on the same square, the efficiency did not increase (\(\eta_\mathrm{s}=3\times 10^{-4}\) to \(3\times 10^{-3}\) versus \(8\times 10^{-4}\)), and the residual-greedy selection remained 2 to 13 times more accurate than the Krylov sampling. Second, we compared cross sections of equal area with integrable and chaotic geodesic flow by Brinkman penalization on a bounding box ( 12). Penalization is a Class I approximation that avoids a conformal map. The sharp interface spreads the solution in the Fourier basis, so the subspaces are larger and the errors higher than with conformal coordinates. The chaotic stadium does not give a higher efficiency than the disk, the ellipse, or the square. In all four cases the residual-greedy selection is about twice as accurate as the Krylov sampling.
